title: ByteDance said to prepare Muse-like agent in push to close AI gap
article:
(Nov 11): ByteDance Ltd plans the release of a Muse-like artificial intelligence (AI) assistant in the coming weeks to augment its lead in AI video, a milestone event the company hopes will help close the gap with top US labs in as soon as three years.

Speaking to its AI team in an all-hands meeting recently, co-founder Zhang Yiming told researchers, engineers and supporting staff about the plan and set out key priorities, according to people familiar with the matter. He sees ByteDance able to compete with leading industry names like Anthropic PBC and OpenAI at the cutting edge, though he cautioned it would take until at least 2029 or 2030, the people said, asking not to be named as the meeting was private.

The planned new AI agent will serve a similar role to Muse, introduced by Meta Platforms Inc in September. Muse has proven a big hit for its US creator, consolidating Meta’s extensive AI research into a voice-based agent with an animated avatar that helps users with various tasks. Meta is distributing Muse across its hardware portfolio that includes various models of smart glasses and an upcoming Muse Charm gadget just for the agent. It’s unclear whether ByteDance also has plans for accompanying hardware.

Top of mind for Zhang, who now spends much of his time working behind the scenes to shape ByteDance’s AI strategy, is data. Zhang, 43, said ByteDance’s Seed large language models (LLMs) are pre-trained on datasets that are orders of magnitude smaller than those used by frontier rivals, according to the people.

Zhang’s comments, which haven’t previously been reported, offered a rare glimpse into the thinking of the entrepreneur behind TikTok and China’s most popular ChatGPT-like bot, Doubao. They reflect his resurgent ambition to dominate an AI arena that China’s most valuable start-up pioneered, but then ceded to the likes of DeepSeek. Central to those endeavours is a plan to spend as much as US$70 billion ($90 billion) and build Seedance into the country’s pre-eminent video AI platform.

A ByteDance spokesperson did not respond to an emailed request for comments.

See also: Businesses see AI gains but remain wary of letting it act alone: surveys

In his meeting, Zhang reiterated his view that ByteDance should not lean on distillation — the practice of exploiting outputs from bigger models to train and improve smaller ones — and must focus on playing the long game. As rivals from Alibaba Group Holding Ltd to Moonshot AI and Z.ai Co advanced their capabilities, they have come in for criticism from White House officials and Anthropic chief executive officer Dario Amodei for distilling leading US models to build up their own products.

Seed is now the only major contender in China’s AI sector that hasn’t yet released an LLM touching the upper reaches of global benchmarks or made its model’s weights — the parameters for steering a model’s responses — available for developers to build on.

The one segment of AI where ByteDance enjoys a meaningful lead is in video generation. The company has leveraged its massive video pool to deliver and monetise a top-tier video-generation model with its Seedance series, filling a void left after OpenAI shuttered Sora.

See also: Sea misses earnings estimates on rising AI costs

ByteDance’s last major LLM update was Seed 2.1, rolled out in June. “There remains room for improvement in the most challenging open-ended tasks and cutting-edge research problem-solving,” the Seed team said at the time. The Financial Times reported in August that the company was training a model with as many as 10 trillion parameters, comparable in scale to Claude Mythos, Anthropic’s top-tier product.

ByteDance is among the most aggressive firms in recruiting and retaining AI talent in China. It offers Seed researchers and engineers preferential equity arrangements that set them apart from the rest of the company.

Seed’s team of roughly 1,000 researchers and engineers is led by Wu Yonghui, whom Zhang poached from Alphabet Inc’s Google DeepMind in 2025. Beyond language, video, and image models, the team is also developing AI for robotics, virtual reality and other hardware. In October, Seed became the first major Chinese AI lab to establish a stand-alone safety and alignment unit, hiring around 10 key researchers.

title: China said to gauge bond interest tax, with yields near record low
article:
(Nov 11): China is sounding out market participants on a possible tax on interest income from government bonds, according to people familiar with the matter, a move that could potentially offer a lift to yields that have been hovering near record lows.

The People’s Bank of China (PBOC), in a survey last month that included a number of lenders, asked how a 25% tax on interest income from their central and local government bond holdings would affect their appetite for such securities, the people said, asking not to be identified as the matter isn’t public. The banks were asked to indicate whether their demand would decline by less than 10%, 20%, 30%, or more than 30%, according to the people.

It’s unclear from the survey whether a levy will be introduced or — if it is — how soon, the people added. Currently, China exempts enterprises and individual holders from interest income tax on these securities.

The PBOC and Ministry of Finance didn’t respond to faxed requests for comments.

Removing the exemptions would fit with the government’s efforts to strengthen tax collection at a time when revenue is weak. It would also elevate Chinese bond yields as investors seek higher returns to compensate for the tax payments. Benchmark 10-year rates have been sliding this year amid angst over subdued domestic economic growth and a slump in the stock market.

See also: China’s tax clampdown brings in US$24 bil from offshore trusts

Yields on China’s 10- and 30-year government bonds reversed earlier declines after the Bloomberg report. Thirty-year government bond futures fell as much as 0.47%, their biggest drop since Oct 30.

“It is always risky when markets are all positioned in one direction,” said Lynn Song, the chief economist for Greater China at ING Bank, adding that policymakers may not want investors to take continued bond gains for granted.

The Chinese central bank, in its third-quarter monetary policy report released on Wednesday, called on investors to take into account the impact of existing income-tax exemptions on government bonds when comparing bond yields with other interest rates. The exemptions allow investors to accept lower yields on government bonds than on other debt subject to income tax, it said.

See also: China extends pause on 24% US tariffs to January, keeps 10% rate

The idea of a tax on interest has stirred debate in the market.

If a 25% levy were imposed and became fully reflected in pricing, that would imply a 52-basis-point increase in 10-year government bond yields to preserve the same after-tax return, according to a tally by local broker Huatai Securities. Huatai expects the actual increase in yields on newly issued 10-year government bonds to be smaller, at around 10 to 20 basis points.

Guohai Securities reckons that imposing a tax just on local government bonds could produce a similar increase in yields — potentially pushing the 10-year yield on local notes to about 2.25% from 1.68%, though the actual adjustment would likely be considerably smaller.

China’s position is a mirror image of that of other major economies round the world, where policymakers have been confronting historically high yields. The PBOC in the past has tried to cool the market when it saw frenzied buying of long-dated government bonds. It’s been vigilant against financial stability risks arising from the bond rally fuelled by leveraged bets, as well as the risk that investor pessimism over the economy’s prospects becomes entrenched because of low yields.

Following a months-long rally that pushed yields to all-time lows in 2024, the central bank mounted verbal pushback against bond bulls, while regulators investigated illegal trading behaviour.

Banks would be particularly exposed to any new levy on bond interest income, as commercial lenders are the biggest holders of China’s roughly 100 trillion yuan (US$15 trillion or $19 trillion) of central and local government bonds. More than 60% of both markets are held by banks, according to Ministry of Finance data.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Changing the tax treatment of sovereign bonds would require an amendment to the law, while that for local government bonds could be done through changes to existing administrative rules.

Huatai estimated that institutional investors would face about 459 billion yuan in additional annual taxes if interest on all outstanding government bonds were taxed. The amount would be roughly one-tenth as large in the first year if the tax applied only to new issuance, according to a report released this month.

Corporate bonds in China are already subject to an income tax. Government bondholders, other than individuals, are also liable for a value-added tax.

Interest on government bonds is currently exempted from corporate income tax. Ending the break would put such payments on a par with corporate income, generally taxed at 25%, as authorities scale back tax incentives to compensate for sliding land-sale revenue. But it also risks raising the government’s funding costs by pushing yields higher — if investors dump bonds.

title: EU targets social media addiction and online ‘dark patterns’
article:
(Nov 11): The European Union is debuting a new plan designed to curb practices that manipulate people into spending more time and money online.

The EU’s executive branch, the European Commission, presented a proposal on Wednesday (Nov 11) for stronger consumer protection rules called the Digital Fairness Act. The measures would give people the ability to switch off online features that encourage compulsive or excessive use, levying fines on companies that violate the rules.

After years of regulating tech companies over issues like antitrust and privacy, EU enforcers are now targeting the key tactics that online platforms use to attract billions of consumers and keep them hooked. These restrictions could have a major impact on the largest social media firms — Google’s YouTube, Meta Platforms Inc’s Instagram and ByteDance Ltd’s TikTok — as well as e-commerce services and artificial intelligence chatbots.

The latest rules would also outlaw “dark patterns" in online sales, design features that nudge or trick consumers into making unwanted choices. These practices can include telling prospective buyers that a product is almost sold out or making it difficult to cancel a subscription.

The new measures could also impact AI bots that encourage users to continue interactions.

“We are making it absolutely clear that false claims about the scarcity of a product or service are a dark pattern and therefore are not allowed,” Michael McGrath, the commissioner in charge of consumer protection, told reporters.

See also: Spain’s main unions hold nationwide strike over housing costs

Alongside the new rules, the EU is claiming new powers to enforce consumer protection rules directly when breaches affect two-thirds of the bloc’s population. Currently, national regulators handle consumer protection violations.

In certain cases, the commission could fine companies as much as 6% of their global annual sales. Smaller businesses would be excluded from direct enforcement, according to the commission.

See also: French grocer Casino agrees to debt deal with opposing creditors

The new proposals will need to be negotiated and approved by European lawmakers and could significantly change before they are passed into law.

title: Singapore Air returns to profit on travel, cargo demand
article:
(Nov 11): Singapore Airlines Ltd returned to profitability in the second quarter as strong travel and cargo demand helped temper elevated costs.

Net income quadrupled to S$210 million in the three months ended Sept 30, the carrier said Wednesday (Nov 11). Revenue climbed 14% to S$5.6 billion on a combination of higher fares, resilient passenger demand and a strong pickup in air cargo volumes driven by the AI boom.

Operating profit, which reflects the airline’s core business, grew year-on-year to S$463 million. Losses from associates, including Air India, shrank by S$110 million from a year earlier. The company does not give a breakdown of its share of losses in Air India, of which Singapore Air owns a 25.1% stake, and is coming off a record loss.

Singapore Air paid S$436 million more than the same time last year in net jet fuel costs, inclusive of hedging. Elevated prices were continuing to place “significant pressure” on the airline, it said.

The war in the Middle East continues to hang over the global aviation industry as jet fuel prices remain elevated. However, average costs fell in the September quarter from historic highs.

See also: Ryanair initiates cost drive to offset US$2 bil fuel surge

Singapore Air has seen an uptick in passengers shifting from the Middle East to Asian hubs. The airline carried just shy of 10.9 million passengers in the quarter, its second-best quarter on record.

The airline was optimistic about demand, pointing to strong seasonal travel flows. Cargo demand has been helped by semiconductor trade, as well as the shifting of some shipments to air freight due to geopolitical and weather-related disruptions to maritime shipping.

The city-state’s flag carrier is betting on flyers embracing premium travel. It’s just unveiled plans for a S$2 billion upgrade to its long-haul aircraft with new seats and other amenities, though Singapore Air has faced online criticism over the colour palette of its new offering.

See also: Thailand puts Bangkok on 24-hour flood watch for IMF meetings

Singapore Air said it would pay a total dividend of S$0.07 per share for the first half, which includes a S$0.05 special interim dividend.

title: Unilever-McCormick deal facing in-depth review from UK watchdog
article:
(Nov 11): Unilever plc and spice maker McCormick & Co’s US$44.8 billion deal faces an in depth investigation unless the firms offer remedies to allay the watchdog’s competition concerns.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said McCormick’s acquisition of Unilever’s global food business can lead to “substantial lessening of competition” in the supply of dry ingredient and sauces in the UK. The two companies have until Nov 18 to offer undertakings to avoid a deeper so-called phase 2 investigation, the CMA said in a statement.

McCormick Shares were down 2.4% by 9am in London, while Unilever remained unchanged.

The decision could potentially create a regulatory hurdle for the ambitious transaction, the biggest in the histories of both companies, but offers the firms a way out. The combination can place Unilever as a global leader in beauty, personal and home care while turning McCormick into a global packaged food business leader.

McCormick agreed to pay US$15.7 billion in cash while Unilever and its shareholders will receive shares equivalent to 65% of the combined company. The transaction values Unilever’s food business at about US$44.8 billion. Unilever shareholders will own 55.1% of the combined company, while Unilever itself will retain a 9.9% stake.

The transaction is part of Unilever chief executive officer Fernando Fernandez’s effort to focus the consumer-goods company on beauty, wellbeing, personal care and home care, businesses that he argues offer stronger growth prospects.

See also: Credit Agricole proposes merging local unit with Banco BPM

Unilever’s best-known food brands include Hellmann’s mayonnaise and Knorr stock cubes, alongside regional brands such as Colman’s mustard and Marmite.

“As announced in August, a decision had already been taken to market the Colman’s brand and assets for sale to proactively address potential competition concerns. Discussions with potential buyers are progressing well,” Unilever said in a statement.

The announcement was an expected step and the two companies were confident in timely closing of the deal, their spokespeople said in separate statements.

title: Türkiye finance chief says climate goals need US$300 bil
article:
(Nov 11): Türkiye will need about US$300 billion of investment to meet its targets on transforming its energy system and lowering greenhouse gas emissions.

The nation has set a target of reaching net zero emissions by 2053 and plans to expand its combined wind and solar capacity to 175GW by 2040, in addition to making investments in energy storage and transmission infrastructure.

“The challenge is can you produce cheap, clean energy so that you can decarbonise the industry? What is doable? How much money is needed? How are we going to pay for it?" Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said Wednesday (Nov 11) at the Global Finance Summit in Antalya, held on the sidelines of COP31.

A real test is finding the resources needed to deliver those ambitions and to balance the challenges of sustaining economic growth while also cutting emissions, he said. Public resources alone will not be enough, making it critical to secure financing from multilateral development banks such as the World Bank Group and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, Simsek said.

“We’ve got plenty of fiscal space but we don’t think public money will be enough for these ambitions,” he said.

Shifting to renewable energy is vital to address dependence on imported fossil fuels, which weigh on the country’s current-account deficit. Energy purchases account for a large share of the country’s current-account deficit, and Türkiye has spent about US$600 billion importing oil and natural gas over the past decade, he said.

See also: EU climate chief rules out fresh finance pledges at COP31

title: China’s tax clampdown brings in US$24 bil from offshore trusts
article:
(Nov 11): China’s ultra-wealthy have declared more than RMB160 billion in back taxes tied to offshore trusts, bowing to pressure from authorities increasingly eager to expand the tax dragnet far beyond their national borders.

The October receipts fuelled an almost 90% surge in national personal income tax revenue for the month, according to the official Xinhua News Agency, which said the vast majority of taxpayers cooperated proactively. Authorities collected over RMB120 billion of the haul in October, with some of the declared amount still to be paid.

The collection marks Beijing’s most aggressive tax enforcement campaign in decades as authorities move to shore up state coffers by targeting the nation’s wealthiest people. High-net-worth individuals were given until late October to pay bills on their overseas trusts without facing extra charges.

The report added that individuals who did not file their taxes or filed inaccurate information may face tax audits and public exposure.

The push followed an announcement in July that China would formally tax offshore trusts set up by its citizens, closing a loophole long used by business dynasties for asset protection and succession planning. Tax authorities also assembled specialised task forces dedicated to auditing the ultra-rich, with some units assigned exclusively to scrutinise individual billionaires, Bloomberg previously reported.

While the revenue collected so far falls well short of the US$100 billion worst-case scenario projected by Barclays analysts for Hong Kong assets, it aligns closely with domestic tax lawyers’ expectations of a US$15 billion to US$25 billion haul. Regardless of the eventual tally, Beijing’s tightening regulatory grip is poised to diminish the appeal of offshore trusts among China’s business elite.

See also: China said to gauge bond interest tax, with yields near record low

The country’s escalating tax grab has fuelled anxiety among the rich, sending individuals scrambling to calculate their liabilities and secure immediate liquidity. Some wealthy citizens have rushed to secure foreign passports over fears that Beijing could introduce an exit tax on emigrants, people familiar with the matter said previously. Others have resorted to liquidating stock holdings or taking out overseas margin loans to meet their tax obligations.

title: Bankers looking at raising Anthropic's valuation to US$1.5 tril or more — FT
article:
(Nov 11): Anthropic PBC’s bankers are weighing plans to increase the company’s valuation in its initial public offering (IPO) to US$1.5 trillion ($1.9 trillion) or more, the Financial Times (FT) reported, a sign of robust demand from investors.

Bankers indicated that they expect to raise the share price above the US$70 to US$78 range announced in a filing on Tuesday, the newspaper said, citing people it didn’t identify. The IPO was fully covered with orders from prospective investors for all the available shares when the deal launched, Bloomberg News has reported.

The Claude chatbot maker and its co-founders are looking to raise as much as US$90.4 billion in the IPO and a private placement, at a market value of US$1.4 trillion, according to the filing. The valuation target reflects the transformative power that many believe artificial intelligence (AI) will have on a wide range of professional activity, and how much of it Anthropic’s tools would potentially be able to replace.

But with the market yet to fully recover from last week’s sharp sell-off in AI-related stocks, investors are now under greater pressure to decide to what degree valuations in the sector represent a plausible trajectory for the new technology.

“Anthropic really represents the first AI pure-play business in the public markets,” said Matt Witheiler, the head of late-stage growth at Wellington Management. “You have AI enablers but you don’t have a native AI company until now.”

In another sign of the building frenzy around the deal, some Anthropic backers are offering a portion of their IPO allocation to new investors. JonesTrading Institutional Services LLC is marketing a block of Anthropic shares of up to US$500 million on behalf of investors who are anticipating sizeable allocations on the deal. The offering is being pitched with a fee of 3% to 5% on top of where the IPO prices.

See also: Alibaba’s chip design unit T-Head files for listing in Hong Kong

The base offering would raise up to US$64.4 billion, according to the filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Anthropic is offering 801.4 million shares, while backers are selling 23.6 million shares. The private placement is set to raise US$26 billion in aggregate, to Advanced Micro Devices Inc, Broadcom Inc, Alphabet Inc’s Google, Micron Technology Inc, Microsoft Corp, Nvidia Corp and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, the filing showed.

Anthropic’s target, including the private placement, would hit roughly US$100 billion when including a so-called over-allotment option or greenshoe, Bloomberg News calculations showed.

The IPO is set to price on Wednesday, Nov 18, and trade the following day, according to terms of the deal reviewed by Bloomberg.

See also: Anthropic IPO buyers see valuation as low as US$1.1 tril

The size of Anthropic’s planned IPO offering including the private placement would be bigger than SpaceX’s US$75 billion base deal, making it the biggest listing of all time. Still, Anthropic’s potential US$1.4 trillion valuation is smaller than Elon Musk’s company was when it made its debut. SpaceX had a US$1.77 trillion market value when it priced its offering.

At the top of the price range, Anthropic would have a market value of about US$1 trillion, based on the shares outstanding listed in the filing. Accounting for employee stock options, restricted shares and stock reserved for the company’s charitable donation matching programme, Anthropic would have a fully diluted value of about US$1.4 trillion.

That ambitious fundraising goal defies jitters from a sharp sell-off in AI-related stocks last week, driven by expectations that politicians promising tougher regulation of data centres and related infrastructure will drive up costs and limit development of the technology.

“Anthropic could justify a US$1.4 trillion market cap if annual recurring revenue reaches at least US$150 billion by 2027, supported by at least US$5 billion of new monthly ARR (annualised revenue run rate) after reporting US$81 billion in October,” wrote Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Mandeep Singh.

Some investors remain sceptical. Jack Selby, who runs the venture capital firm Copper Sky and is a managing partner in Peter Thiel’s family office, warned that the deal may become the catalyst for a major reversal in the AI trade. Selby, a long-time sceptic of the AI trade who more than a year ago called the euphoria surrounding the industry the biggest bubble yet in private technology investing, warned that the Anthropic lock-up expirations could particularly pressure shares.

“An underperforming Anthropic IPO has to be a very prominent player in what will be a pretty massive correction in the market with respect to AI,” Selby said in an interview on Bloomberg Television on Wednesday. “If the most anticipated AI company’s IPO falls very short of its projected valuation, and just imagine where it’s going to go after the lock-ups expire.”

The widespread adoption of Claude Code and rival tools by software developers points to the impact many expect it to have, from discovering new miracle drugs to navigating complex legal and accounting rules to running a factory. Already, more than 90% of contributions to Anthropic’s code base were written by Claude, the filing showed.

Anthropic has introduced so-called vertical solutions in these areas, with particular emphasis on healthcare and life sciences. It counts Novartis AG chief executive officer Vas Narasimhan as one of its board members.

The company’s seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, are offering 3.38 million shares each in the IPO, the filing showed.

It is planning a live-streamed event, at which Amodei will discuss the Claude chatbot maker’s IPO with JPMorgan Chase & Co CEO Jamie Dimon on Friday, Bloomberg News reported.

Sales are surging. The company reported a revenue run rate of US$81 billion as of Oct 31, up US$10 billion from the end of September, the filing showed. Anthropic had a US$65 billion run rate figure at the end of July, Bloomberg News reported. Anthropic defines the metric as annualising consumption-based fees for a trailing 28-day period and subscription-based fees for a single month.

“The company is on pace to be at or within a small distance of growing 10-times year-over-year for three years in a row,” Wellington’s Witheiler said. “That’s never happened before.”

“This brings balance to the AI supply and demand picture which hasn’t been apparent in the public market thus far,” he added.

Goldman Sachs Group Inc research analysts are modelling for Anthropic revenue to soar to roughly US$685 billion by the end of the decade, Bloomberg News reported.

Anthropic reported third-quarter revenue of nearly US$17 billion as of Sept 30, versus US$1.4 billion in the same period a year ago, its filing showed. On Monday, Anthropic unveiled new versions of its powerful Mythos and Fable models, both of which are faster than prior versions, while Fable is less expensive, as some companies cut back on their spending on the technology.

Keeping the pace of development running at a break-neck pace will require growing revenue faster than Anthropic’s spending on AI infrastructure. Anthropic’s commitments climbed to nearly US$901 billion in the latest filing, most of which are for computing power, chips. About US$71 billion worth — a figure that’s larger than the individual market caps of roughly two-thirds of S&P 500 companies — are due just in the year through Sept 30, 2027.

Unlike other tech companies with sources of income such as advertising to fall back on, Anthropic will have to convince investors that its focus on AI alone will generate profit far beyond the technology’s surging costs. SpaceX may have tied its aspirations to AI when it pitched investors on its IPO, but most of its actual revenue at the time came from its other business lines.

That hasn’t stopped asset managers, venture capital firms and some of the biggest tech companies from backing Anthropic to the tune of tens of billions of dollars. Funds scattered across investment houses including Fidelity Investments, Capital Group and BlackRock Inc and venture capital firms such as Iconiq, Spark Capital and Sequoia Capital hold Anthropic shares before the IPO. Alphabet Inc’s Google, Amazon.com Inc and Microsoft Corp are backers as well as customers and key suppliers of computing power.

title: Volkswagen EV sales in China climb to monthly record in sign of turnaround
article:
(Nov 11): Volkswagen AG said its namesake brand’s sales of electric vehicles (EVs) and hybrids in China climbed to a record last month, and forecast that growth will continue this year as its turnaround efforts in the world’s largest auto market start bearing fruit.

October deliveries of EVs and plug-in hybrids — a category known as new energy vehicles (NEVs) — surged nearly 350% from a year ago to more than 28,000 units, Volkswagen said on Wednesday. New models — including the ID. Aura T6 sport utility vehicle and the ID. Era 5S sedan — drove the increase.

The company said it expects to sustain growth in the coming months, with a goal to rank among the 10 bestselling NEV brands in the country next year.

The results represent a rare green shoot in China for Volkswagen, which recently reported that its ventures in the country had turned unprofitable as it fell further behind local brands in China’s overcrowded auto market. As part of its efforts to catch up, the manufacturer plans to introduce more than 20 new electrified models in the country this year.

The company has increasingly turned to Chinese partners to accelerate its transformation and offer cars catering to local tastes. Its collaboration with Xpeng Inc has produced a new EV architecture, while a software partnership with Horizon Robotics has added new self-driving capabilities.

Still, the automaker will have to show it can generate sustained volume growth in China’s ultra-competitive EV segment after a period of bruising declines in the country’s shrinking auto market.

See also: Audi and Mercedes hit by walkouts in union push for higher wages

Volkswagen’s group deliveries in China fell 30% during the first nine months of the year. Fully electric vehicles represented just 3.5% of the group’s sales there in the period, underscoring the gap between Volkswagen’s electrification ambitions and current market position.

title: South Korea fines bond dealers record US$1.2 bil over collusion
article:
(Nov 11): South Korea’s antitrust regulator imposed a record 1.63 trillion won (US$1.2 billion or $1.6 billion) fine on more than a dozen domestic banks and brokerages for colluding in sovereign bond auctions, exposing a yearslong practice that undermined competition and raised the government’s borrowing costs.

The primary dealers exchanged bid-yield information or agreed on yields and volumes in 150 Korean Treasury Bond auctions from January 2020 through June 2023, the Korea Fair Trade Commission said in a statement Wednesday. It found that the dealers reached agreements on specific bid yields or volumes in 145 auctions among them in South Korea’s roughly 1,261 trillion won market.

KB Securities, Korea’s fourth largest brokerage by total assets, was hit with the biggest fine of 332.2 billion won, or about a fifth of the total penalty, followed by NH Investment & Securities and Mirae Asset Securities. The fine was widely expected, though the amount was lower than some analysts had estimated.

The investigation found dealers coordinated so-called “goalpost yields” — bids designed to help meet their underwriting obligations while avoiding actually buying the bonds. The practice carried risks: if the auction reached those yields, dealers could end up with more bonds than they wanted.

According to the commission, dealers shared and compared those levels with rivals ahead of auctions and, in some cases, agreed to submit bids at the same or similar yields. The practice reduced uncertainty over competitors’ bidding strategies and weakened competitive pressure in the auction process.

See also: US Treasuries stumble as strong jobs data backs Fed-hike bets

“We believe reduced competitive pressure in government bond auctions led to an artificial increase in auction yields,” FTC Standing Commissioner Kim Gun-sung told reporters in a briefing Wednesday.

The practice was so entrenched that when employees changed roles, they handed their successors contact details for rival dealers and even used manuals setting out how to communicate with competitors during different stages of an auction, Kim said.

The financial penalties may not be the end of the fallout.

See also: Google debt-risk gauge rises as earnings revive AI debt jitters

The regulator also filed criminal complaints against seven firms, including Mirae Asset Securities, NH Investment & Securities, Industrial Bank of Korea, KB Securities, Kiwoom Securities, Korea Development Bank and Korea Investment & Securities, with the Serious Crime Investigation Agency.

The crackdown is expected to promote competition in the government bond issuance market, where barriers to entry are high, and improve the efficiency of public financial management, the FTC said. Despite the regulatory action, the dealers can continue operating as usual, with any decision on their primary-dealer status left to the finance ministry, the commission added.

The association of primary dealers, which is currently chaired by NH Securities, was not available for immediate comment. The ruling is preliminary and the institutions can appeal to the commission or the court.

The case echoes a series of collusion scandals that have swept through global fixed-income and currency markets over the past decade. European regulators fined investment banks in 2021 over a cartel involving European government bonds, while UK authorities last year imposed penalties after finding traders at major banks unlawfully exchanged sensitive information involving government-bond trading and auctions.

The FTC’s penalty is the largest ever imposed in a cartel case in Korea, according to the commission, surpassing the previous record of 747.6 billion won levied on starch makers earlier this year.

South Korea had 18 primary dealers as of June 2023, when the FTC’s probe started, and 15 of them were penalised by the commission this time, according to the statement.

Primary dealers are finance-ministry-designated banks and securities firms that participate directly in government bond auctions. The market is dominated by domestic banks, which underwrite, trade and hold government debt in return for benefits including noncompetitive purchase rights and funding support.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

“We fully took into account concerns that the market could shrink,” FTC’s Kim said, adding that the finance ministry’s views on the potential impact on the government bond market were considered when setting the penalties and applying reductions.

A spokesperson for the finance ministry declined to comment.

Despite the regulator’s action, shares of most brokerages penalised in the case rose Wednesday, while NH Investment & Securities and Samsung Securities fell 3.7% and 0.8%, respectively on the Korea exchange.

The fines are large enough to weigh on the shares of some of the bigger brokerages, Seol Yong Jin, an analyst at iM Securities, said.

“Compared with earlier talk of trillion-won fines for individual firms, the outcome is something of a relief,” Seol said. “Still, the penalties are likely to affect earnings at several brokerages for the first-half of 2027, and the decline in shares of firms such as NH Investment & Securities suggests the market is already pricing in some of the impact,” he added.

Kim said the commission also weighed the firms’ financial capacity and broader market conditions, while acknowledging uncertainty over how the market would respond. He added that the case could ultimately have a positive effect by prompting a rethink of a market dominated by a small group of players.

title: UK PM's rejection of EU financial rules shows Brexit reset limit
article:
(Nov 11): Andy Burnham’s government won’t accept so-called dynamic alignment of the UK’s financial services rules with those of the European Union (EU), a stance that raises questions about the prime minister’s wider ambitions for closer ties.

Under the mechanism, the UK would automatically follow EU regulations in certain areas. But as ministers seek to maintain the City of London’s independence, the Burnham government does not want it to apply to financial services, UK officials told Bloomberg.

The UK’s Labour government is in talks with the EU to forge closer ties that may include alignment in sectors such as agriculture and energy, but British officials have told EU counterparts that applying it to financial services is a red line they are unwilling to cross, people familiar with the matter said. All spoke on condition of anonymity because talks are ongoing.

While the development will be welcomed by some in the City of London who have welcomed post-Brexit freedoms including the removal of a cap on bankers’ bonuses, it also highlights complications involved in Burnham’s push for a much closer EU relationship. If he were to try to take Britain back into the EU or join its single market, as he has said is possible, he would likely have to sign up to its rules governing financial services.

A UK government spokesperson said it would not provide a commentary on its negotiations with the EU but stressed that Britain’s financial services are a key national strength. The UK’s opposition Conservatives and Reform UK parties have long opposed dynamic alignment, saying it would leave Britain as a rule-taker with no say over devising regulations.

British banks took a hit after the UK voted to leave the bloc in 2016, but the divergence in regulations over the last decade means much of the sector now opposes alignment of its regulations.

See also: Brits snap up hand sanitiser, canned food on stockpile advice

In July, TheCityUK, which represents Britain’s financial services industry, said automatic dynamic alignment “is not appropriate for the UK’s financial and related professional services industry”. It argued that the sector “requires the UK regulatory authorities’ speed of decision taking, flexibility and agility, and could not operate effectively under arrangements that require it to automatically follow the lead of another jurisdiction with different priorities and needs”.

A paper published by UK Finance in June said “we do not support wholesale UK alignment or dynamic alignment with the EU in financial services”, arguing that Britain’s post-Brexit divergence meant it could now respond more swiftly to risks and market developments, and that its rules should be “tailored to domestic conditions”. The group argued that the UK had benefitted from diverging from the EU on environmental, social and governance disclosures, digital assets and artificial intelligence.

Burnham is maintaining the position held by his predecessor Keir Starmer’s government, which exempted financial services from a push for closer alignment with the EU, some of the people said. They said dynamic alignment on financial services was not included in a paper of common understanding agreed between Starmer’s administration and the EU in 2025.

See also: Bank of England may raise high-risk mortgage threshold, FT says

Anand Menon, a director of the UK in a Changing Europe think tank, told Bloomberg that the Bank of England and the Treasury would always be likely to oppose “rule taking” in financial services, helping explain Burnham’s decision to reject dynamic alignment.

He said Burnham’s stance would appear to rule out the so-called Norway option for a future relationship, which would allow single market membership through the European Economic Area but without voting rights on rules.

Instead, according to Menon, Burnham appeared to be considering a more bespoke Swiss-style arrangement, though he cautioned that may not be on offer from the EU. The other option to avoid becoming would a rule-taker would be to rejoin the EU in full, Menon said, as then Britain would then be able to have a say on the bloc’s regulations.

title: An 800 mil jobs gap in the developing world fans new risks
article:
(Nov 11): Developing economies face an employment gap of 800 million jobs over the next 15 years as a generation of young people reach working age and the nations have limited resources to tackle the challenge, according to the World Bank Group.

About 1.2 billion people in the emerging world will pass the age of 18 over the period, while the countries are forecast to create only around 400 million new jobs, President Ajay Banga said Wednesday at the Climate Finance Summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

The gap has “profound consequences for poverty and prosperity, for migration, for stability”, he said at the event, being held as nations gather in the resort city for the annual United Nations-convened COP31 climate talks.

“There’s rising debt, conflict, challenges with resiliency of infrastructure, and natural disasters, so their resources to meet their development ambitions are increasingly constrained,” Banga said.

In the year through June 30 the bank mobilised a total of US$230 billion ($295 billion) into the developing world, including US$112 billion in private capital — a threefold increase on fiscal 2022, according to the institution.

See also: US loses grip on US$121 bil mobile gaming sector to China

While mobilisation rates were higher across lower-middle income countries and in upper-middle income countries, the flow of capital was flat in low-income countries, Banga said. “That’s the issue, the challenge of reaching the poorest markets and it kind of reinforces the importance of public resources for those lowest income countries,” he said.

Emerging economies also need better development models to improve resilience to the impacts of climate change — to protect coastlines, safeguard harvests, and deliver infrastructure able to withstand severe weather, according to Banga.

“We’re trying to bring together the combination of what we call smart development — build physical resilience and institutional strength into development from the very beginning,” he said. “A flood resistant road keeps trade moving without being rebuilt twice, an insulated school gives children learning through extreme heat.”

title: Spain’s main unions hold nationwide strike over housing costs
article:
(Nov 11): A national strike impacted transport and other public services across Spain on Wednesday (Nov 11), as unions demand for more affordable housing.

The 24-hour general strike was called by the country’s two main union umbrella groups after two government-sponsored housing bills were rejected in Parliament in early October. The protest has broad support from administration officials, including Labour Minister Yolanda Díaz, a member of the junior coalition partner who has strong ties to unions.

Electricity demand was 10% lower than usual at 8am local time, a smaller drop than during similar previous strikes, when the decline was higher than 14%, according to CEOE, Spain’s main industry group. Pickets have caused disruptions to the access to the port of Algeciras — one of Spain’s main hubs — as well as at industrial sites in major cities including Barcelona, Valencia and Seville, CEOE said.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who faces an election on Nov 29, has had a strong relationship with unions since he came to power in 2018. Wednesday’s strike is widely seen as politically motivated and aimed at the right-wing parties that are expected to win the Nov 29 ballot. It is unclear how much support it will have from workers.

Sánchez called the snap election after his bills were rejected, betting that he could present himself as a defender of social rights seeking to solve the housing crisis, which has seen prices surge under his watch.

Spain had not seen a general strike of this kind since 2012, when the country was in the midst of a crisis that ravaged the economy. In 2018 and 2019, unions called general strikes to coincide with International Women’s Day, but protests were only held for two hours.

See also: EU targets social media addiction and online ‘dark patterns’

A separate protest by train drivers on Tuesday caused disruptions for commuters in Madrid and other major cities as strikers failed to comply with mandatory minimum services. Train drivers have been demanding better safety conditions for months, and tensions have intensified after a recent high-speed train accident killed 69.

On Wednesday, strikers formed pickets outside bus stations across the country. Police charged against protesters at Madrid’s wholesale food market early in the morning, Cadena Ser radio station reported.

title: Sony bets on homegrown anime to fuel decades of future growth
article:
SEOUL (Nov 11): From the Walkman and PlayStation to Spider-Man’s box office records, Sony Group Corp has shown a knack for shaping global pop culture hits. Now in the midst of a strategic transition, the company is pouring time and money into a homegrown genre with the potential to power growth for decades to come: anime.

After turning Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba into a global phenomenon, the company is working to seed or acquire the next anime blockbuster. Some 80 years into its history, Sony is determined to create franchises that will last about as long.

The US$28 billion ($35.9 billion) anime industry is one of the fastest growing genres of entertainment globally. For Sony, it’s a key part of a broader shift away from relying on physical hardware like the PlayStation console and towards IP and content. Much as with beloved game characters transcending their original format, hit anime franchises become gold mines not only for viewership but also for merchandise, music and live experiences.

“With Demon Slayer, it is our intent to make this last 10 or 20, if not 50 to 100 years,” Atsuhiro Iwakami, president of Sony Music Entertainment Japan and chairman of Aniplex, Sony’s anime production company, said in an interview. He points to Dragon Ball and One Piece, stories that have survived long enough to pass from parents to children and which Sony has rights to stream internationally. “We want to make sure we’re part of creating the type of franchise that can withstand decades.”

Tokyo-based Sony has turned anime into a scalable business in recent years with acquisitions of services like Crunchyroll, now the world’s largest streaming platform dedicated to the genre. It’s become a go-to destination for fans, who’ve grown from a niche group to a much larger contingent with the help of various celebrities and music artists embracing the genre.

The proof of the concept for Sony came with the Demon Slayer saga, depicting the adventures of a young swordsman battling demons while trying to restore his cursed sister to human form. Its 2020 movie, Mugen Train, became Japan’s highest-grossing film, dethroning Studio Ghibli’s 2001 classic Spirited Away. Five years later, the first instalment of Demon Slayer’s Infinity Castle trilogy grossed about US$800 million worldwide, demonstrating that a franchise born from Japanese manga could become a global theatrical blockbuster.

See also: SoftBank shares fluctuate after US$7 bil loss on writedown

The distinctly Japanese aesthetic and storytelling style, far from hampering international appeal, was a big part of the attraction.

At the centre of Sony’s push to do more with anime is Iwakami, who’s been with Aniplex since its inception and has helped shape its trajectory over almost three decades. He’s part of the strategic collaboration inside Sony to turn Aniplex and Crunchyroll into a complementary duo, where one produces and the other distributes original content.

Iwakami’s defining bet was to combine the visual craftsmanship of ufotable, a studio known for spectacular anime aimed at what he calls “geeks or nerds”, with the mass appeal of manga from Weekly Shonen Jump. That experiment delivered Demon Slayer.

The underlying Demon Slayer IP still belongs to Japan’s century-old manga publisher Shueisha, whose titles also include One Piece, Dragon Ball and Naruto. Asked whether Sony might invest in closely held Shueisha to gain greater access to its rich IP, Iwakami left the possibility open. “Perhaps, if the opportunity presents itself,” he said.

Japanese entertainment companies are often competitors and collaborators at the same time, making takeover deals complicated.

“So it’s not necessarily the case that just because we want to buy something, we can actually make that happen,” Iwakami said. “But if timing and chance align, we would certainly be open to entertaining different types of M&A.”

Sony’s taking steps toward becoming an IP powerhouse. Last year, it became the largest shareholder in Kadokawa, owner of a vast library of manga, novels and games. It’s also trying to create more IP from scratch. Securing the franchises and storylines that build enduring appeal is becoming increasingly competitive as streaming giants such as Netflix Inc and Walt Disney Co also compete for anime licensing deals.

Aniplex and Crunchyroll formed a new studio, Hayate, focused on developing and producing original anime for global audiences. The two also announced plans to adapt more stories into Japanese anime and live action by collaborating with homegrown creators, giving Sony another route to build franchises.

The logic is straightforward. Anime has traditionally relied heavily on production committees, where publishers, studios, broadcasters and other partners share the cost, risk and rights. Greater control of the foundational IP could give Sony more freedom, and potentially more of the economic upside, as it takes a hit story across streaming, games, music, merchandise and live experiences.

Sony put that ambition on display in New York in October. On the eve of New York Comic Con, about 500 creators, executives and other industry players gathered at the Javits Center for Crunchyroll’s first Anime Future Forum. Sony chief executive officer Hiroki Totoki opened the event, flanked by executives from PlayStation, Sony Pictures as well as Iwakami. Director James Gunn, actor Samuel L Jackson and musician Big Sean took part in discussions.
