The message was clear: Anime is becoming a central piece of Sony’s effort to knit together its sprawling entertainment businesses.

The audience Sony's chasing filled the convention centre. Fans of Nintendo Co’s Super Mario, orange-clad Naruto followers and stormtroopers in full uniform mingled with One Piece pirates in straw hats and sword-carrying Tanjiros from Demon Slayer. Elaborate wigs, capes and prop weapons bobbed through the crowds as thousands of fans descended on Comic Con. Japanese anime, once a niche, spilled into every corner of the venue.

Sony has more ways than most rivals to turn that fandom into a business. Aniplex can produce anime; Crunchyroll, with 21 million paid subscribers, can take it to viewers around the world; PlayStation can turn anime into games or games into anime; and Sony Music’s core operations can extend franchises into soundtracks, concerts and merchandise, helping to turn a successful anime into something much larger than a television show or movie.

“Anime has a high affinity with the film and gaming businesses, making it an important sector for Sony as it aims to grow as an entertainment platform,” said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Masahiro Wakasugi. “Furthermore, anime theme songs may positively contribute to Sony's music business, and the IP of anime protagonists can serve as medium- to long-term assets. Alongside games, music, and movies, anime is expected to hold an essential position as entertainment content.”

Iwakami is also ready to imagine an audience beyond the action-heavy anime that fuelled much of the industry’s global rise. He wants to explore animation for children and families, pointing to Bluey and Japan’s Chiikawa as examples. Sony has also increased its ownership of Peanuts Holdings to 80%, giving it control of Snoopy and other characters with appeal across generations and markets.

Even a Sony theme park — like Disney or Universal’s — is a possibility.

“To make a theme park, I think having control of IP is a prerequisite and necessary,” Iwakami said. If Sony eventually has enough demand and enough control of its characters, “then we can look into something that big”.

But before Sony can extend anime into ever bigger businesses, it faces a more basic constraint: Japan is struggling to make enough of it. Looking back to 20 years ago, Iwakami recalls an anime could go from planning to broadcast in about a year — but today it can take three to four years. Skilled animators are scarce, costs have risen and the painstaking human craftsmanship that gives Japanese animation its distinctive character makes production difficult to accelerate.

Sony is investing in training young animators while engaging with local governments on ways to build infrastructure for developing talent, Iwakami said. He also sees technology as part of the answer. He is cautious about generative artificial intelligence, saying it should support the artists behind anime rather than displace them.

“There will be tools that will assist,” he said. “But it is not our goal to replace any of these creators.”

That willingness to experiment has defined Iwakami’s career. A Hollywood movie fanatic and Gundam fan who collected Gunpla models, he says Sony has given young producers unusual freedom to test ideas. Early in his career, he thought less like a corporate executive than an individual producer pursuing projects that seemed fun and worth trying.

Three decades later, he is trying to preserve that culture on a much larger stage.

“Sony has always been intertwined with the evolution of technology and entertainment,” Iwakami said. He wants to see the company spark another unpredictable leap in the tradition of the PlayStation, which Sony's domestic music arm helped bring about by merging its entertainment mindset with hardware engineering. “It’s my hope that someone among the ranks will emerge and take on a new challenge that will produce results and grow the business in areas that you and I can’t predict.”

title: SoftBank shares fluctuate after US$7 bil loss on writedown
article:
(Nov 11): SoftBank Group Corp shares fluctuated as investors assessed its quarterly net loss and a US$3.7 billion ($4.7 billion) writedown over its US data centres, against newfound optimism around artificial intelligence (AI).

The stock fell as much as 11% in early trading in Tokyo. The Japanese tech investor said Tuesday it swung to a ¥1.12 trillion (US$7.1 billion or $9 billion) loss in its fiscal second quarter after writing down non-refundable advance payments it made to secure power-generation equipment for its US data centres.

The stock rose as much as 0.8% in the afternoon as the sentiment for the sector got a boost from better-than-expected earnings from AI computing provider CoreWeave Inc and a report that Anthropic PBC’s bankers are weighing plans to increase the company’s valuation in its initial public offering.

“What investors worried about most this past week was whether data centre investment would slow,” said Toshiro Sato, a chief executive officer at Kyokuto Securities Research Institute. “SoftBank’s results came as everyone was anxious about that business. After the selling ran its course, the reassessment came through and the stock is coming back.”

SoftBank had previously hurried to secure the equipment it needed for AI data centres, sometimes even before long-term plans were finalised, chief financial officer Yoshimitsu Goto said during an earnings conference.

Total payments for power-generation equipment hit US$9.5 billion by September, he said. The company said in its earnings statement that it can receive rebates of up to US$2.1 billion over the next 10 years on future equipment purchases. SoftBank is conducting “a thorough reassessment” including a review of its procurement strategy, Goto said, without going into specifics.

While part of the loss is due to accounting, “the real issues are a ¥597 billion power-equipment write-off that raised more questions” than what the management could explain, and the financing costs that grew 2.6 times year-on-year, Jefferies analyst Atul Goyal wrote in a note. “Management is playing defence.”

SoftBank shares have plunged more than 50% from their record high in June, among the worst performers on the Nikkei 225 Stock Average for the period. Volatility, meanwhile, has risen as investors sought to gauge the risks and opportunities around its AI investments.

title: Nintendo sold 5.2 mil copies of ‘Zelda’ remake in four days
article:
(Nov 11): Nintendo Co sold 5.2 million copies of its The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake in just four days, invigorating the Switch 2 platform that had been waiting for a blockbuster hit.

Released on Nov 5 for US$59.99, the 2026 edition is a complete recreation of the 1998 classic action-adventure game for the Nintendo 64 console, replete with new graphics, level and character designs. It ranks among the best-reviewed video games of recent times, earning a score of 96 out of 100 from both players and professional reviewers on aggregator Metacritic.

The Switch 2 console has had an uneven first year on the market, challenged by the rising cost of memory pushing hardware prices up. The fast start by the new Ocarina of Time takes the Zelda game past the cumulative sales of Donkey Kong Bananza, another popular title from 2025. Only Mario Kart World, which was part of a launch bundle with the Switch 2 console, has sold more units so far.

The first Switch, released in 2017, got a huge boost from having The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild as a launch-day title that helped draw in gamers from outside the Nintendo ecosystem. Though a remake, the new Ocarina of Time may have a similar effect as Nintendo heads into the crucial holiday season.

title: ABN Amro profit jumps as acquisition, interest rates lift income
article:
(Nov 11): ABN Amro Bank NV reported a 52% jump in quarterly profit that was fuelled by higher interest rates and a recent acquisition. The dutch lender also lifted the outlook for its biggest revenue source for the second time this year.

The Amsterdam-headquartered bank posted net income for the three months through September of €939 million (US$1 billion), according to a statement on Wednesday. That compares with €617 million in the year-ago period.

ABN Amro’s shares have gained about 46% this year as chief executive officer Marguerite Berard overhauls the lender and the European Central Bank’s tighter monetary policy rates buoys revenue. The Dutch government has pared its financial crisis-era holding in the lender, partly helped by rising valuations.

With the recent acquisition of NIBC Bank NV, Berard has sought to boost the lender’s footprint in the Dutch retail market. She is also focused on keeping a lid on costs by offloading a personal loan business, outsourcing a chunk of the bank’s credit card business and slashing jobs.

The bank’s largest shareholder, the Dutch state, last month announced plans to sell-down its stake to 10.5% through a trading plan. Berard touted the move as “additional proof of the confidence the Dutch government has” in the bank.

Net interest income — the difference between what the bank earns on loans and pays on deposits rose 15% in the third quarter, partly due to contributions from NIBC, growth in client deposits and financing demand from the bank’s clearing clients. Fees were 7% higher in the period.

See also: Siemens Energy sees 2030 profit surge on gas power demand boom

The lender now sees commercial net interest income for the year at above €6.9 billion, up from the €6.8 billion it had previously forecast.

ABN Amro projects costs to remain at about €5.5 billion in the year. The bank said it has already achieved about half of its 2028 job cut target.

Berard said the bank started the fourth quarter “with good business momentum” and that it will update its targets next quarter.

title: Siemens Energy sees 2030 profit surge on gas power demand boom
article:
(Nov 11): Siemens Energy AG said profit margins will swell to as much as 22% by 2030 after the company more than doubled earnings last year on booming demand for gas turbines and power-grid equipment.

The German maker of gas turbines and transformers expects annual revenue growth to average as much as 14% through fiscal 2030, the company said Wednesday as it reported results for fiscal 2026.

Siemens Energy has benefitted from the global surge in energy demand driven by the build-out in AI infrastructure and electrification. That has pushed its backlog to record levels, though investors have grown more cautious over whether the AI infrastructure boom can continue at the same pace.

For the current fiscal year, the company sees higher margins, net income of about €5 billion (US$5.6 billion) and free cash flow before tax of roughly €10 billion.

Siemens Energy’s gas services unit has been one of the biggest beneficiaries of the power boom. The company expects growth at the unit to accelerate again this year as demand for large turbines remains strong, particularly in North America. Data centre customers account for more than a quarter of sales at the business.

See also: SPH Media is latest Singapore firm impacted by data breach, report says

Profit before special items more than doubled to €5.5 billion in fiscal 2026, ahead of analysts’ expectations, as the company converted more of its backlog into higher-margin sales. Its margin jumped to more than 12% from 6% a year earlier.

Free cash flow before tax nearly doubled to €8.8 billion, helped by customer advances and reservation fees as buyers sought to secure capacity.

The company is also returning more cash to shareholders, announcing late Tuesday an additional share buyback of as much as €9 billion through fiscal 2030, on top of an existing €6 billion programme. On Wednesday, it proposed more than tripling its dividend to €2.30 a share.

See also: Vodafone raises profit forecast after cost cutting campaign

The larger shareholder returns aim to reassure investors after concerns about the sustainability of the data centre boom weighed heavily on the stock. Siemens Energy shares have fallen roughly 36% since touching a record high in April. The stock had increased more than 10-fold from the start of 2024 through that peak.

Siemens Gamesa also reached breakeven for the full year, a milestone in a turnaround that has taken years following quality problems and mounting project costs. The wind-turbine division posted a small profit before special items, compared with a nearly €1.4 billion loss a year earlier.

“We will capitalise on strong markets and execute our record backlog with discipline, while allocating capital with the same rigor,” Chief Financial Officer Maria Ferraro said in a statement.

Siemens Energy is also reshaping its portfolio. In August, the company said it would prepare its Transformation of Industry business for independence, with options ranging from bringing in outside investors to a potential listing or sale.

title: Malaysia to start electricity market for data centre operators
article:
(Nov 11): Malaysia intends to launch a separate wholesale electricity market for large power consumers, including data centres, the New Straits Times reported.

The existing single-buyer market serving households, factories and commercial premises will stay the same, the newspaper said, citing Rumaizi Abdul Halim, director of market regulation and planning at Malaysia’s Energy Commission. The two markets will run under a single operator but details on how they would interact will be discussed later, he said on Tuesday.

The move underscores Malaysia’s efforts to deal with the potential fallout from its ambitious push to become a regional hub for data centres. The Southeast Asian country has attracted artificial intelligence investment from technology heavyweights, including Oracle Corp and Amazon.com Inc, while Alphabet Inc’s Google said last week that it plans to spend US$15 billion to expand data centre and cloud operations in Malaysia.

title: Indonesia to cut 300 more tightly held stocks from benchmark
article:
Indonesia’s bourse more than quadrupled the number of stocks found with high shareholder concentration, as it sought to resolve MSCI Inc.’s complaints about illiquidity and opaque ownership.

The Indonesia Stock Exchange said 300 more stocks have been identified, adding to the 83 on a list to be excluded from gauges. The latest group made up about 6% of the benchmark index’s market capitalisation, it said without naming them or when they will be removed from the gauge.

While the move represents the Southeast Asian country’s accelerated response to MSCI’s warning last month that it faces a two-step downgrade from emerging markets status, analysts said it still falls short of addressing the fundamental issues plaguing local equities. While authorities have tightened rules after MSCI’s complaint first emerged in January, the index compiler said they weren’t sufficient, laying out the need for enforcement actions.

“We see this directionally positive as IDX now detects concentration at source rather than reacting to prices,” said Wilbert Arifin, analyst at PT Mirae Asset Sekuritas Indonesia, but adding that the move “does little for the case.” “What matters is the list shrinking through actual sell downs and more enforcement regarding coordinated trading behaviour,” he said.

The announcement, made by Indonesia Stock Exchange Chief Executive Jeffrey Hendrik late Tuesday, is the latest step by regulators to stave off a double downgrade by MSCI. Authorities have also imposed fines on manipulative market practices and pledged strong enforcement.

See also: Prabowo said to accept Indonesia vice president resignation

The exchange will remove the market-cap prerequisite for inclusion on the list, previously set at 5 trillion rupiah ($277 million), and introduce new qualifying criteria. These include stocks where 10 or fewer holders own at least 92.5% of shares. The bourse will also drop the so-called price impact ratio, which measures the magnitude of a share move relative to its trading activity, as a determining factor.

Firms that are on the list will be removed from both the MSCI and JCI indexes. To exit the list, firms and shareholders have to sell stock to the public via transactions in the regular market.

The clutch of companies previously identified for closely-held shares include tycoon-linked PT Barito Renewables Energy and PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa.

See also: Thailand EV tax gets carmakers weighing more local production

MSCI said it welcomes feedback from market participants on the reclassification proposal until April 30 and will announce its decision on or before June 30.

The move comes as Indonesian stocks have suffered months-long foreign outflows, with the benchmark gauge tumbling more than 40% this year to become the world’s worst performer. The Jakarta Composite Index fell 0.2% on Wednesday morning.

In a note after the announcement, Citigroup Inc analysts including Ferry Wong said that recent actions by authorities are decent, “but more efforts are likely needed to avoid downgrade.”

title: US loses grip on US$121 bil mobile gaming sector to China
article:
(Nov 11): Yang Liu’s parents planted roots in suburban Michigan hoping their son, who was born in China, would find success in the world’s biggest economy. In early 2020, they got their wish: End Game Interactive, the mobile game startup he co-founded in their home, raised US$3 million on the back of breakout hit Zombs Royale.

Then, the US still commanded a major slice of what is now a US$121 billion global industry thanks to games like Temple Run, Plants vs Zombies and Pokemon Go. But now, Liu is one of a generation of American game designers despairing as Chinese studios churn out games that are faster, cheaper and able to extract more spending from players. Operating costs in the US are now so high that Liu is building out his business in Latin America, where he employs more than 40 people.

“It’s extraordinarily hard for startups like ours — despite having an incredible amount of capital — to find individuals to compete on the global stage, which gaming has become in the past 10 years; and one in which the US is no longer the dominant force,” Liu said.

China’s advance has been rapid. As recently as early 2024, the US and China were virtually neck-and-neck in terms of revenue share from the world’s top 100 mobile games, according to data from Sensor Tower. But by mid-2026, China held 40% of the global market, compared with just 16.5% for the US, as the Asian nation dominated the charts with hits like Honor of Kings and Whiteout Survival.

In a cruel twist, China’s biggest overseas market last year was the US itself. Chinese titles account for over 18% of revenue from the top-100 games there, up from 8% at the start of the decade. At the same time, the share held by US publishers has shrunk from 40% to less than 30%.

See also: Canada looking at relief from US tariff after Trump’s midterm election loss

China’s gains on the US in sectors ranging from AI to electric vehicles, solar panels and drug development, are well-documented. While the mobile gaming sector gets less attention, it is the fastest-growing part of the global games industry and eclipses both Hollywood and music streaming in terms of revenue.

Mobile games’ ubiquity — more than three billion people will play them this year — means they are an understated but potent channel of soft power. The highly stylised fantasy and anime characters that dominate top Chinese titles now anchor the daily digital feeds of Gen Z and Gen Alpha, underscoring the broader departure from American cultural hegemony.

It has left developers in the US grappling with existential questions around how to compete with China’s extensive supply chain and unmatched development speeds. In a nod to the structural shift at play, some top American developers like Microsoft Corp’s Activision Blizzard and Take-Two Interactive Software Inc’s Zynga are using Chinese studios to make their games.

It is not just China taking a share from the US. Studios in Singapore have produced Garena Free Fire. Turkish startup Dream Games has the popular Royal Match puzzle game and a swell of M&A activity has underpinned rapid growth in recent years. In the second quarter, publishers from those two countries combined accounted for 18% of revenue from the top 100 games in the US, up from 1.2% in the first quarter of 2020, according to Sensor Tower.

Meanwhile, Finland is a global gaming hub that’s produced Angry Birds, as well as some of the world’s current top titles like Supercell’s Clash of Clans and Clash Royale. Still, there’s no escaping China’s reach; Supercell has been majority owned by Tencent Holdings Ltd since 2016.

In February, Supercell CEO Ilkka Paananen issued a call for innovation to close the gap with Asian companies. Of the 22 games launched since 2020 that had grossed at least US$1 billion, 20 were from developers in China, Japan, and South Korea. Just two were developed in the West: Royal Match and Monopoly Go, he said.

“We in the West should look in the mirror,” he said in a blog post. “The fact is, we have not brought radical new gameplay innovation to the market.”

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

For many years, Chinese studios released what were essentially copies of popular foreign games, known as reskins, or free-to-play versions that had shorter sessions and lower graphics quality. But much like in EVs and other consumer products, China’s ability to build out the supply chain and harness a huge pool of cheap labour has underpinned its rise to global prominence.

China’s huge domestic audience of about 680 million gamers also means developers have finessed how to make money by the time they release a game internationally.

By mid-2026, Chinese titles generated about US$47 in quarterly revenue per active user in the US market. That is nearly six times the US$8 average for American games — a threshold that’s stayed relatively stagnant over the past decade.

For many in the industry, Genshin Impact, released in September 2020 by China’s MiHoYo, is a rubicon. The free-to-play role-playing game came three years after Nintendo Co released Zelda: Breath of the Wild and built on what had drawn fans to the blockbuster hit — windswept fantasy worlds, plucky but powerful protagonists — to become a quick-moving sensation on smartphones, PCs and PlayStations.

Crucially, the game managed to monetise its audience of millions, though its methods saw it pay US$20 million to settle a claim in the US that it used a convoluted and chance-based system to obscure the true cost of prizes in so-called loot boxes.

Still, it has earned US$6.2 billion from mobile gamers alone, showing that a high-budget, anime-style open-world game could be a hit in the West. Most recently, MiHoYo games were featured in ads for Apple Inc’s new iPad mini and iPhone Duo.

MiHoYo’s developers are “like economists and psychologists making video games,” says Robert Wynne, co-founder of Rising Tide Studios, which develops games in China. “They’ve mastered player behaviour where they know exactly what you want and when.”

But the leading Chinese force is Tencent, now the biggest gaming company in the world. In just the first half of 2026, its Honor of Kings is estimated to have earned US$1 billion and, more than a decade after its release, is helping drive a double-digit increase in Tencent’s domestic game revenue. Niko Partners estimates that Honor of Kings has grossed over US$30 billion since it was released.

“Which US game company can go against Tencent today, head-to-head? None,” said Liu. “Against NetEase? None. Even against MiHoYo? None.”

More recently, China’s push for growth has shown there is money to be made from women gamers — a segment in which Western companies have been slow to gain traction. Love and Deepspace, in which a female protagonist is wooed by anime men with artfully tousled hair and smouldering eyes, has raked in more than US$60 million in some months since its launch in 2024 by teasing new romantic scenarios that are locked behind paywalls.

Meanwhile, the American industry is a shadow of its former self.

Last year, Electronic Arts shut down seven mobile games made by Glu Mobile, the mobile-gaming company it bought for US$2.1 billion in 2021.

Microsoft has only released a trickle of new mobile games after its US$69 billion purchase of Activision Blizzard in 2023, which gave the software company the long-running hit Candy Crush. At the time, Microsoft said that the acquisition was aimed at accelerating the growth of its mobile gaming business.

Representatives from EA, Zynga, Tencent and Microsoft declined to comment. NetEase and MiHoYo did not provide comment when contacted by Bloomberg News.

In a sign of the times, hits like Call of Duty Mobile and Diablo Immortal were made in China, partially for Chinese gamers, though Microsoft owns those titles. A Blizzard spokesperson told Kotaku for a 2018 story on this that Diablo Immortal had been developed for both Western and Eastern markets and that one of the company’s core values is to think globally.

Worldwide, Chinese publishers now produce 40 of the top 100 titles, up from 21 a decade ago, while US publishers have fallen to 13 from 22, according to Sensor Tower.

With Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund scooping up Scopely and Niantic, that leaves just a handful of American-owned and -based developers remaining.

American firms looking at overseas markets face hurdles in China. A tricky regulatory environment effectively boxes them out of the market that’s expected to generate US$41 billion by 2030, according to Niko Partners. In the first half of the year, the National Press and Publication Administration approved 1,110 domestic video games for Chinese consumers and just 37 from international game developers.

That lopsided access has been a longtime bugbear of Western countries which, after years of relative openness, are tightening access to Chinese technology. The US has investigated Tencent over its stakes in Riot Games and Epic Games, and the company has been designated as a Chinese military company — a classification it denies.

But talent is where China really has the edge.

Salaries are the biggest expense for game companies and game makers. They pay, on average, US$142,000 for every developer in the US, according to a survey by the Game Developers Conference. In Shanghai, where salaries tend to be higher, the average game developer earns about US$50,000 a year, according to data from Glassdoor.

“Salaries have been rising in the West and there’s a bit of complacency on top of that,” says Jens Hilgers, the founding general partner of Bitkraft Ventures, an investment platform for gaming. “In the East, you have people who are getting more hungry, who are understanding, ‘How do I develop for global markets and Western markets?’”

US mobile game makers are trying to adapt.

Some are opting out of the free-to-play model and asking gamers to pay for games despite widespread reluctance around upfront purchases. Globally, just 16 games appear in the top 100 lists for both downloads and revenues.

Others are shifting from mobile platforms to the open web, where Apple and Alphabet Inc’s Google cannot extract fees from every purchase — a headwind for US developers in particular. In China, game developers are tapping into the popularity of apps like WeChat and Douyin as platforms to develop so-called mini games.

Still, Liu says it’s a pessimistic outlook despite America’s status as a top country for business and entrepreneurship.

“Seeing a country that blessed me with so many opportunities undergo such a decline in the industry I am in, and that I love — is deeply sad.”

title: China’s iron ore buying clout makes each deal a market event
article:
(Nov 11): State-backed iron ore buyer China Mineral Resources Group Co has had a good year, securing deals with two of its biggest suppliers that establish its dominance of a market worth north of US$100 billion.

But success could present new challenges. The agreements struck with Australian mining giants BHP Group and Rio Tinto Group are not permanent. BHP will need resetting as early as next year. Smaller rival Fortescue Ltd is still wrangling over terms. The negotiations themselves could now become a recurring price risk.

Introducing centralised iron ore purchasing for China’s sprawling steel industry minimises the number of negotiations but each one becomes much more important. Bargaining over pricing and which benchmarks to use, contract durations and settlement currency are now confined to a single track of high-stakes talks.

“The risk now sits in discrete events: bans, easings and settlements that can move prices within a single session,” said David Cachot, iron ore analyst at Wood Mackenzie Ltd. “CMRG has introduced a greater degree of event-driven risk linked to negotiations, trade restrictions and procurement directives.”

CMRG was set up in 2022 to represent the world’s largest steel industry, which buys more than 70% of the world’s seaborne iron ore, converting it to about one billion tonnes of metal a year. Beijing had long complained about the profitability gap between the big miners and the mills that rely heavily on imported ore, particularly from Australia and Brazil.

See also: China copper crunch puts industry on defensive as costs soar

Pooling all that purchasing power has given CMRG much greater leverage in talks that were previously conducted between individual miners and steel companies, allowing it to challenge how prices are set and in what currency.

Ultimately, the goal is lower costs for mills. The company has made a big effort to consolidate market data to improve its understanding of supply and demand. Last week, it unveiled artificial intelligence agents to track vessels and capture price differentials and inventory levels at ports.

But the negotiations have been tense, creating uncertainty and volatility in a once predictable market. The months-long standoff with BHP saw unofficial restrictions on its ore that pushed up prices. Fortescue has taken a more combative approach and, with product curbs in place, has warned its operations could be affected if talks stretch beyond the end of the year.

See also: Copper extends rebound as global technology stocks resume rally

Rio Tinto reached its accord with less friction, agreeing on a longer contract that runs through May 2028. Meanwhile, Brazil’s Vale SA has managed to evade term deals for now, sticking with spot contracts due to its different product mix.

A Rio Tinto spokesperson said the company does not comment on details of confidential commercial negotiations but noted its “long and successful relationship with our customers in China". BHP and Fortescue declined to comment. CMRG didn’t respond to a request for comment.

If the government extends CMRG’s remit, other commodities markets that depend on China might soon find themselves wrestling with an unfamiliar playbook. Flush from its success in iron ore, the company’s next target could be copper or another metal.

Iron ore futures in Singapore slipped 0.9% to US$91.75 a tonne as of 10.27am local time, dropping for the third day. Prices in Dalian were down 0.8%.

The dispute with BHP showed that worries over possible disruptions can raise prices — particularly on futures markets that attract speculators — even before actual supply is materially affected. That’s arguably helped keep iron ore prices higher than they should be this year.

It means that both sides may have reason to favour longer agreements.

“Downstream participants value above all the predictability of raw material costs,” said Zhong Hong, a researcher at Citic Futures Co. “Multi-year frameworks support production planning, profit budgeting and long-term volume commitments, and reduce operational volatility stemming from sharp spikes and collapses in spot prices.”

And the balance of power could shift quickly between talks. CMRG has negotiated over the past year against a backdrop of weak Chinese steel demand, pressure on mill margins and new supply from Guinea’s Simandou project. In later rounds, those conditions might have changed.

“Pricing power is less permanent than it looks,” said Sushmita Vazirani, lead iron ore analyst at Kpler. “If the market tightens again, through supply disruptions or a demand recovery, leverage would swing back toward the miners.”

“The structure has changed but the balance of power is still cyclical,” she said.

title: China copper crunch puts industry on defensive as costs soar
article:
(Nov 11): China’s copper crunch is squeezing activity and margins at the firms that shape the metal into wires, rods and tubes for use in products from cables to electronics and consumer goods.

The surge in domestic prices is forcing many fabricators to operate on a hand-to-mouth basis, only buying the raw material once they have secured an order for a finished product. The cost of copper, a metal ubiquitous across supply chains, is just one aspect of roaring inflation at Chinese factories, which accelerated last month to the highest level in over four years.

“We basically only do back-to-back business,” said Zhang Benben, sales engineer at Ningbo Shimao Copper Industry Co, which supplies cabling for solar panels and electric motors. “We only buy copper cathodes to produce after we receive sales orders.”

While the Iran war and heavy spending on artificial intelligence have pushed up costs for energy and metals generally, the global copper market is also feeling the impact of the Trump administration’s protectionist tilt. China has struggled to replenish its stockpiles because so much metal has been diverted to the US in anticipation of import tariffs.

Copper has hit successive records this year, though a recent rout in AI stocks has pared some of those gains on concerns over the outlook for data centre spending. The metal rose 0.8% to US$13,788.50 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange as of 10.21am Singapore time.

See also: Copper extends rebound as global technology stocks resume rally

The premiums paid to import and buy copper in China, the world’s biggest market, have hit record levels in recent weeks. Shipments of refined metal have weakened this year, while higher ore costs and poor margins have forced domestic smelters to cut output.

Copper fabricators struggle to influence prices because, like many industries in China, there is too much capacity relative to demand. Customers can choose the best deals and margins are often razor thin.

The constraints on supply are occurring against the backdrop of a deeply uneven economy, where household consumption is tepid but exports are booming. Certain sectors that rely on copper, such as solar, are seeing resilient demand as developers rush to meet year-end targets.

See also: Asian rice price climbs near two-year high in inflation threat

But even when orders are holding up, the dislocation in price is causing problems. At Zhejiang Baichuan Conductor Technology Co, which supplies copper wire to the solar industry, the firm is getting squeezed because it pays upfront for cathodes while its customers buy on credit, said sales executive Yang Xun.

Shimao Copper has also tightened up on payments from customers and will not give extensions beyond due dates, said Zhang.

High prices typically spur substitution. Baichuan Conductor has benefited from selling copper-clad aluminium wire, which solar producers are testing as a replacement for pure copper wiring to cut costs, said Yang. Usage has not been scaled up yet because there is not a national standard for the product, he said.

The Chinese copper industry may catch a break after the Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections undercut the case for both massive AI spending and US President Donald Trump’s tariffs. The recent pullback in international prices could help loosen the market as it becomes more profitable to ship metal to China, said Wang Wei, general manager of Shanghai Wooray Metals Group Co, a trading house that sells to fabricators.

title: Global policies target data-centre grid delays, lower emissions
article:
(Nov 11): Governments around the world are looking for ways to speed up data centres’ connections to local power grids, seeking to curb a growing reliance on on-site natural gas plants that threatens to increase emissions from the boom in artificial intelligence, according to BloombergNEF (BNEF).

Data-centre developers are increasingly turning to so-called behind-the-meter power generation to bypass years-long waits for grid connections and get their facilities running sooner. Those systems typically rely on natural gas, potentially reversing years of progress in cutting emissions from electricity generation.

A report published Wednesday by BNEF examines proposed policy efforts in the US, Europe and Asia to accelerate grid connections and limit the environmental impact of data-centre growth.

“Powering data centers via the grid today would result in lower CO2 emissions than using on-site gas in the US and Europe,” the report’s authors wrote. “Keeping data centres connected to the grid in developed markets is therefore a core pillar of keeping them green.”

BNEF’s report comes as the annual UN Climate Change Conference, COP31, gets underway in Antalya, Türkiye. The environmental footprint of data-centre expansion is expected to feature in discussions among world leaders, government officials and financial industry executives seeking ways to accelerate the transition to cleaner energy.

Bankers have already said AI will be part of “every conversation” at the summit. Even so, the scale of AI’s climate impact remains difficult to quantify. Data-centre electricity demand is likely to quadruple by 2035, reaching about 7% of global power consumption, according to BNEF estimates.

See also: Cohere in a ‘fight’ to secure AI computing power

The BNEF report, commissioned by Bloomberg Philanthropies, assessed seven different policy types aimed at speeding up data centres’ grid connections. Four showed strong evidence of accelerating those connections, while only two were found to have a direct impact on increasing the supply of clean energy for data centres.

“The bottom line here is it depends on what each power market needs,” said Musfika Mishi, a BNEF analyst and co-author of the report.

For example, at PJM Interconnection, the largest US grid operator, there is a huge deficit in supply, so the company is “prioritising policies that get data centres connected to the grid faster, but also bring supply to the grid,” she said.

See also: Nvidia scandal underscores growing espionage risks for AI firms

Not every policy analysed in the report is explicitly designed to make data-centre power supplies cleaner, Mishi said. But in developed markets, connecting to the grid is generally better for the climate than relying on on-site generation, she said.

The report also acknowledges that most policies to speed up grid connections are too new to assess how much they actually shorten wait times or reduce emissions. Still, the policies proposed represent an important step towards addressing the challenge of expanding data-centre capacity without driving up greenhouse gas emissions.

“You’ve got a balance between affordability, reliability and sustainability, that classic trilemma. And I think in recent years there’s been a bit more focus on affordability and reliability rather than sustainability,” said Derrick Flakoll, a BNEF analyst and co-author of the report. “I would say that in certain places like the US, where you’ve had different election results, those are going to continue to be big themes.”

BNEF also examined data-centre growth in developing markets, where the challenge is often shifting power systems towards cleaner energy while expanding the infrastructure needed to serve new demand.

In India, for example, that means adding local transmission and substation capacity fast enough to keep pace with data-centre development. In Malaysia, data-centre growth is expected to increase reliance on existing coal and gas plants in the near term.

title: Cohere in a ‘fight’ to secure AI computing power
article:
(Nov 11): Cohere Inc chief executive officer Aidan Gomez pushed back on concerns about overbuilding AI computing capacity, saying his startup faces a daily struggle to procure the power it needs to run its operations.

The Canadian startup, an Nvidia Corp.-backed developer of artificial intelligence models for businesses, is confronting shortages of what the industry calls compute, the sheer computational power needed to churn through the training and operation of models. Without its own data centers, Cohere depends on cloud providers like the big names like Microsoft Corp’s Azure or the so-called neocloud providers like CoreWeave Inc.

“We really have to fight to get access to compute,” Gomez said in an interview with Bloomberg in Tokyo on Wednesday. “There is a dearth of supply. We need much more compute. We need the energy, the facilities, the chips to support that.”

Gomez is visiting Japan this week to help expand Cohere’s business with Japanese enterprise customers and government agencies. His comments underscore demand for AI chips and processing, which was also highlighted by CoreWeave’s robust earnings overnight. CoreWeave reported better-than-expected sales of US$3.66 billion for the September quarter, helped by growing relationships with clients including Cohere.

“We might be over-indexing to fear in this present moment, but hopefully the build-out continues, and those supply pressures do alleviate,” Gomez said.

He’s added his voice to a global debate about the intensity of spending on building out AI data centres, which are coming in for greater skepticism as costs rise, projects run into unforeseen challenges and communities increasingly protest the setup of such facilities in their locales. SoftBank Group Corp on Tuesday announced it was writing down US$3.7 billion in costs associated with its US data centre projects, as the company best known for its investments transitions into a hardware and infrastructure developer.

See also: Nvidia scandal underscores growing espionage risks for AI firms

Toronto-based Cohere, which seeks to sell its services in support of countries pursuing sovereign AI, last month raised as much as US$5 billion in a funding round valuing it at more than US$20 billion.

Cohere and Nvidia are working together to develop custom AI models optimised for the US chipmaker’s platforms. Gomez described the recent revelations about Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s infidelity as “a really unfortunate episode” — one that would deal a great blow if he’s forced to step down from his post. Huang’s extramarital affair is being probed by the FBI and Nvidia-appointed independent investigators over allegations it may have been with a Chinese spy.

“Any change of leadership, especially with someone as effective, and with such a strong vision as Jensen would be quite disruptive,” he said. “Jensen has been leading the company for 30 years, it’s his vision that really carried it to the place that it is today.”

title: SPH Media latest Singapore firm impacted by data breach — report
article:
(Nov 11): Singapore publisher SPH Media was hit by a cyberattack, local media reported, just days after hackers accessed tens of thousands of flight bookings at national carrier Singapore Airlines Ltd.

SPH Media said mainly email addresses, names, mailing addresses and phone numbers were compromised in the cyber-attack incidents detected between Nov 4 and Nov 8, CNA reported. Financial or banking information was not compromised.

The incident marks the latest in a spate of cyber breaches impacting companies in Singapore this month.

Singapore Airlines reported that hackers accessed data on about 46,000 flight bookings stored by Amadeus IT Group SA last week. School meal ordering application Tappee was hit by a breach, catering services provider SATS Ltd said on Tuesday.

Other recent data breaches include those at telehealth provider Doctor Anywhere and telecommunications company M1 Ltd.

title: Nvidia scandal underscores growing espionage risks for AI firms
article:
(Nov 11): Nvidia Corp chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy has underscored how Beijing and other nations are increasingly turning to corporate espionage to gain an edge in the global artificial intelligence race.

The Nvidia scandal has erupted as another recent AI spying case unfolds in the US courts: an OpenAI engineer from Saudi Arabia faces charges of planting a hidden recording device in one of the ChatGPT maker’s executive conference rooms. In January, a federal jury also convicted a former Google engineer of stealing AI trade secrets for China.

Former officials and intelligence analysts warn the incidents highlight the growing risks to private sector firms as the global competition for artificial intelligence heats up — and foreign nations make it a priority for spies and industrial espionage efforts.

“The AI companies are increasingly becoming targets of foreign intelligence services,” Chris McGuire, a former White House official in charge of technology competition with China now at the Council on Foreign Relations. “If you want insight into what’s happening in the most sensitive US technology areas, you don’t go infiltrate the Department of Commerce. You infiltrate Nvidia and OpenAI.”

Nvidia, the world’s second most-valuable company, has said an investigation by its board will address recent reports that its CEO “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

The firm at the centre of the global AI boom has said it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. Jensen Huang said he would cooperate fully and that he is committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security.

See also: Nvidia intervened in US probe of Megaspeed chip smuggling

US President Donald Trump said the FBI is looking into Huang’s extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, but offered his support to the celebrity executive, who has travelled the world extolling the virtues of AI.

“I just know Jensen very well,” Trump said. “I just think he’s a very honourable man.”

China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun has denied suggestions that China spied on the Nvidia chief through Alice Huang, who met the world’s preeminent AI industry executive as the founder of Megaspeed International. Her firm was the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia — a major route for smuggling the firm’s advanced hardware into China.

See also: Nvidia shares drop after CEO Huang’s affair triggers board probe

Nvidia’s dominant position in the high-end chip market gives it unique insights into a technology seen as increasingly crucial to the modern economy — as well as for an edge in advanced military applications.

China’s top spy agency would likely have tasked Alice Huang with a range of priorities, including securing information about Jensen’s private conversations and corporate plans, according to former intelligence officials and analysts. The Nvidia chief’s close ties to Trump would also make the CEO an appealing target.

“To be able to ask Jensen covertly what he saw, what he thought, what are the conversations he heard from other global leaders” at places such as the White House “is going to be humongous for China,” said William Evanina, former director of the National Counterintelligence and Security Center, which leads the US government’s efforts to counter foreign spying.

Another likely task by China’s Ministry of State Security would have centred on more deeply penetrating Nvidia’s supply chain by pushing deals with compromised subcontractors and encouraging the hiring of other Chinese operatives, said Evanina, who also led counter-espionage efforts at the Central Intelligence Agency.

He added that Alice Huang may also have tried to influence Jensen’s views on specific chip contracts and global policy issues of importance to China. The Nvidia chief has long pushed to relax export controls on China and allow the company to export advanced chips there.

Alice Huang’s firm, Megaspeed International, has previously denied allegations that it helped China evade export controls.

A bulletin posted by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence’s Counterintelligence directorate in late October warned government and business leaders about the risks of Chinese espionage tactics.

“When partnering with any foreign entity, US state and local government and business leaders should exercise caution, conduct thorough vetting, and build transparency and accountability into partnership agreements to guard against the risk of foreign government exploitation,” the note said.

Back in April, Republican Senator Jim Banks of Indiana warned about the growing Chinese espionage threat in a letter sent to a group of AI industry CEOs that included OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic PBC’s Dario Amodei, but not Jensen Huang.

title: Keppel Infrastructure Trust to acquire 70% of Keppel Sakra Cogen from Keppel Asia Infrastructure Fund
article:
On Nov 11, Keppel Infrastructure Fund Management (KIFM), the Trustee-Manager of Keppel Infrastructure Trust (KIT), announced that KIT is proposing to acquire 70% interest in Keppel Sakra Cogen Plant (KSC), Singapore’s first hydrogen-compatible combined cycle power plant from Keppel Asia Infrastructure Fund (KAIF) for approximately $111.6 million. Following the Proposed Transaction, KIT and Keppel’s Infrastructure Division will hold 70% and 30% interests in KSC respectively.

KSC will operate under a 30-year availability-based capacity tolling agreement with Keppel’s Infrastructure Division. Under the arrangement, capacity payments are based on plant availability, providing stable and predictable contracted cash flows and substantially insulating KSC from merchant power price and fuel supply risks. KSC's day-to-day power generation operations will continue to be performed by Keppel’s Infrastructure Division under a long-term operations and maintenance agreement.

The consideration is based on the long-term capacity tolling agreement and operations and maintenance agreement underpinning cash flows. Before completion, KSC expects to refinance its existing debt facilities with new debt facilities of approximately $650.0 million. Based on the agreed equity value and projected net debt following the refinancing, the implied enterprise value of KSC at completion is over $780 million on a 100% basis.

Located on Jurong Island, Singapore, KSC is Singapore's first hydrogen-compatible combined cycle power plant and has generation capacity of 600 MW. Developed by Keppel’s Infrastructure Division, KSC incorporates advanced technology and design features that make it one of the most energy-efficient power plants in Singapore.

The plant commenced commercial operations on May 29 and currently runs on natural gas, with the ability to co-fire up to 30% hydrogen at the outset.

Kevin Neo, CEO of KIFM, said, “KIT is pleased to acquire a strategic stake in the Keppel Sakra Cogen Plant, strengthening KIT’s investment in Singapore’s essential energy infrastructure. KSC is highly complementary to the Keppel Merlimau Cogen (KMC) Plant in KIT’s portfolio. Together, they have a combined generation capacity of 1.9 GW and feature hydrogen-ready technology, supporting Singapore’s energy security and resilience. The Proposed Transaction is expected to be DPU accretive to KIT Unitholders.”

See also: The new risk equation for infrastructure

The Trustee-Manager intends to fund the consideration with a combination of internal sources of funds and/or external borrowings of KIT.

The Proposed Transaction is subject to obtaining of regulatory approvals, and approval from unitholders of KIT at an extraordinary general meeting (EGM) to be convened.

title: Asian stocks rise on AI enthusiasm, bonds decline
article:
(Nov 11): Asian stocks climbed after better-than-expected earnings from CoreWeave Inc revived interest in the artificial intelligence trade, helping offset a Wall Street sell-off fuelled by hotter-than-expected US inflation.

The MSCI Asia Pacific Index rose as much as 0.8%, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 gaining 0.8% and South Korea’s Kospi advancing 0.6%. Contracts for the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 rose 0.6% in early Asian trading, reversing much of the losses for the underlying index in regular trading.

CoreWeave shares rose about 2% in late trading after reporting quarterly earnings that topped analysts’ estimates and boosting its annual forecast. The results signalled that sales growth remains strong at the AI computing provider despite challenges facing the data centre industry.

Anticipation is also building ahead of Anthropic PBC’s listing as the firm targets US$1.4 trillion ($1.8 trillion) in fully diluted market value through its initial public offering.

Yields on benchmark government bonds in Australia and New Zealand rose at least five basis points each following a sell-off in Treasuries. There’s no trading in cash Treasuries on Wednesday as the US is closed for a holiday. A gauge of the dollar was little changed after rising 0.5% on Tuesday, while crude oil steadied after a two-day decline.

In the US, S&P 500 snapped back-to-back gains after consumer prices, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3% in October from a month earlier, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data, topping estimates for a third straight month. Overall CPI jumped 0.4% as the cost of essentials climbed across the board.

See also: Asian stocks climb as tech rallies, oil slips

The data triggered a sell-off in Treasuries, with the rate-sensitive short-dated bonds hit the hardest. Two-year yields jumped 17 basis points to 4.73%, the most in 19 months. Money markets are now pricing in the Fed to raise rates by a quarter point at its meeting next month, with some chance of an even larger move. Futures are baking in about three quarter-point hikes by June.

Following the release of CPI data, Dallas Fed president Lorie Logan said more rapid rate hikes may be needed this winter to calm inflation. Her remarks followed earlier comments from governor Christopher Waller that a half-point rate increase in December may be warranted. Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee said officials have to address the elevated inflation, calling the October report on consumer prices disturbing.

“The Fed could push for a more-aggressive tightening cycle with CPI continuing to print strong,” said Lindsay Rosner at Goldman Sachs Asset Management. “A December hike is our firm base case despite wider AI jitters, and stubborn inflation means we cannot rule out further hikes in 2027.”

See also: Asia hedge funds, rich investors face big losses in AI rout

The prospect of aggressive Fed hikes threatens to derail a nascent recovery in stocks that were whipsawed in the wake of Democratic sweep of the US Congress in the midterms. For bonds, the sell-off marked a reversal of a rally that began early last month as tech stocks slipped on worries about the sustainability of the artificial-intelligence boom.

Meantime, shares of SoftBank Group Corp tumbled as much as 11% in Tokyo after it swung to a ¥1.12 trillion (US$7.1 billion or $9 billion) loss in its fiscal second quarter, following a US$3.7 billion writedown for its US data-centre projects and falling AI valuations.

Elsewhere, US oil steadied after a two-day decline. On Tuesday, Brent crude settled below US$92 a barrel on expectations of further de-escalation in the Iran war. Brent is still up almost 50% this year but the oil market has seen a dramatic turnaround in November, with prices tumbling from a six-month high.

title: Nvidia board members tap Wachtell’s Kim for Huang probe
article:
(Nov 11) : Nvidia Corp.’s independent board members tapped a former top federal prosecutor to help probe Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

The chipmaker’s board directors retained Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz partner Joon H. Kim “to conduct a thorough and independent investigation,” according to a brief statement Nvidia issued Tuesday. Kim previously served as acting US attorney for the Southern District of New York.

Nvidia’s board announced the probe on Sunday, saying it was assembling a committee of independent directors to explore reports of Huang being targeted for foreign intelligence. The move coincided with an explosive admission by the CEO that he’d had an affair with a woman the US government reportedly suspects of spying for Chinese intelligence.

The matter has sent shares of Nvidia, once the world’s most valuable company, plummeting on speculation that Huang will have to step down or that the company will face greater regulatory or legislative scrutiny. It’s also engulfed the White House, as Huang developed a close relationship with President Donald Trump, who personally invested in Nvidia and signed off on the sale of its chips to Chinese entities

Nvidia shares initially fell further Tuesday afternoon following the company’s announcement that it was retaining Kim but recovered somewhat by end of the trading day. Wachtell is one of New York’s most elite law firms, and Kim has a strong reputation as a dogged investigator.

Michael McGovern, a former federal prosecutor now at Ropes & Gray, called Kim a “phenomenal choice,” noting that New York Attorney General Letitia James tapped him to probe the sexual harassment claims that led to Governor Andrew Cuomo’s resignation.

See also: Asian stocks, bonds to drop as Fed hike bets mount

“His conclusions are unimpeachable and supported by the evidence,” McGovern said of Kim. “He leaves no stone unturned.”

Huang had previously said there was nothing inappropriate about his relationship with the woman, who worked for a Singapore-based customer. Nvidia has also said it has no reason to believe either US national security or corporate secrets were compromised.

One of New York’s most prominent corporate law firms, Wachtell is perhaps best known for its public-company mergers and acquisitions work. It recently served as lead counsel for Warner Brothers Discovery Inc. in its US$111 billion acquisition by the company now known as Skydance Corp. Wachtell’s litigation group has also handled many high-profile disputes, including representing the former Twitter Inc. in its 2022 suit demanding that Elon Musk honor his offer to buy the social-media site for US$44 million.

See also: OpenAI third quarter revenue soars nearly 50% to US$10 billion

In Kim, Nvidia’s board has chosen a veteran federal prosecutor who served as the top deputy to former Manhattan US Attorney Preet Bharara. Kim was part of Bharara’s team in his insider-trading battle with the former SAC Capital, which pleaded guilty in 2013 and agreed to pay a US$1.8 billion penalty. Earlier in his career, Kim was part of a series of prosecutions of relatives of former mob boss John Gotti.

Kim took over as Manhattan’s top federal prosecutor on an acting basis after Trump fired Bharara shortly after the start of his first term. Kim left that office in January 2018 and became a partner at the law firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton. He and James led the Cuomo probe in 2021, while he was at Cleary. Their report found that Cuomo sexually harassed current and former state employees and presided over a “toxic” and “emotionally abusive” executive chamber. Cuomo stepped down shortly after.

Kim only recently joined Wachtell from Cleary. He came in months after Wachtell’s co-chair and veteran litigator William Savitt departed to another firm, Gibson Dunn & Crutcher, along with five other partners.

title: OpenAI third quarter revenue soars nearly 50% to US$10 billion
article:
(Nov 11) : OpenAI’s quarterly revenue hit US$10 billion for the first time in the three months ending in September, according to a person familiar with the matter, driven by strong demand for its latest artificial intelligence software.

The ChatGPT maker’s revenue increased nearly 50% from the prior quarter and nearly threefold from the same period a year earlier, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the information is not public. The financial details were shared with investors during a call on Tuesday.

After slipping behind longtime rival Anthropic PBC this year by some measures, OpenAI has regained momentum with competitive new AI models, aggressive price cuts and a greater focus on AI agents to help customers automate work. OpenAI’s business has shown signs of accelerating at a moment when Anthropic’s revenue growth has begun to slow somewhat.

Anthropic, which is nearing a landmark Wall Street debut, reported third-quarter revenue of about US$17 billion. The rate of growth from the second quarter slowed to around 47%, compared to a more than 140% increase in the previous quarter. (OpenAI and Anthropic have historically calculated revenue figures differently.)

OpenAI is in the process of completing a new round of funding at a US$1.25 trillion valuation after delaying plans to go public until next year. OpenAI recently completed an initial US$11 billion part of that round, Bloomberg News previously reported.

See also: Stocks, bonds fall as Fed-hike chorus grows louder

Anthropic is targeting a US$1.4 trillion valuation for its public listing later this month.

title: Stocks, bonds fall as Fed-hike chorus grows louder
article:
(Nov 11) : Wall Street doubled down on wagers the Federal Reserve will need to lift rates more aggressively, with stocks and bonds falling as inflation worries spurred fresh warnings from officials.

A strong consumer price index fueled bets on a quarter-point December Fed hike, with traders projecting some chance of a larger move. Treasury two-year yields jumped the most since April 2025. The S&P 500 halted back-to-back gains. The dollar rose. In late hours, CoreWeave Inc. gave a solid outlook, easing fears about the debt-laden business suffering a slowdown.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a half-point December hike may be needed. That was followed by remarks from Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, who backed at least two more quarter-point increases, adding those may be necessary at a quicker pace than officials have moved.

“The Fed could push for a more-aggressive tightening cycle with CPI continuing to print strong,” said Lindsay Rosner at Goldman Sachs Asset Management. “A December hike is our firm base case despite wider AI jitters, and stubborn inflation means we cannot rule out further hikes in 2027.”

Even if the Fed decides to lift rates by a quarter point at its upcoming meeting, the risk of stickier near-term inflation argues for hiking at both the December and January meetings with the risk of another in March, according to Tiffany Wilding at Pacific Investment Management Co.

“A Fed policy rate hike in December appears quite likely and the question is more about whether it will be a quarter point hike or a half point,” said Rick Rieder at BlackRock.

See also: Stocks climb as buyers step in despite Nvidia woes

While financial conditions have been adjusted by markets in rapid fashion, inflation still stayed very high on the minds of openly communicative Fed officials over the past couple of weeks, he added.

“With the near-term trend looking worse, a December Fed hike is a given unless financial conditions tighten materially further or markets are very volatile on the eve of the meeting,” noted Krishna Guha at Evercore. “The larger question is why inflation has come in hotter in recent months, and what this means for policy in 2027.”

A December hike looks locked in, but an outsized move should require evidence that inflation is accelerating decisively, expectations are becoming unanchored or the economy is overheating, said Seema Shah at Principal Asset Management.

See also: Asian stocks brace for selloff as AI rout deepens

“We are not there yet,” Shah noted.

title: Wall Street bonuses seen climbing before prospects weaken
article:
(Nov 11): Wall Street is poised to deliver another banner year for bonuses off record profits for big banks, with questions lingering around what lies further ahead for the industry.

Year-end compensation packages are projected to rise 20% to 30% or more for traders who help investors make stock bets and bankers who help companies raise capital in the equity market, according to Johnson Associates Inc. It would be the third straight year financial firms have doled out higher payouts.

“The banks continue to do better than anticipated” in what has been “a very good year” driven by momentum in markets in recent months, Alan Johnson, managing director of Johnson Associates, said in an interview.

While the good times are still rolling, Johnson said he’s cautious about the outlook for 2027. With only a handful of stocks driving much of the trading, underwriting and advisory activity, the momentum may not stay elevated, he said.

“After three good years in a row,” he said, “I think we’re less optimistic about repeating that for the fourth time.”

See also: IBM to end immigration sponsorship for roles in biggest unit

The projections for 2026 signal that incentive pay will potentially be up on Wall Street by the most ever. Last year’s payouts came on the heels of the highest annual profit the largest US banks had seen since 2021. Those firms are now on track to deliver record earnings again.

Investment bankers who arrange deals could see their pay increase as much as 20%, according to Johnson Associates. That comes as advice for arranging mergers and acquisitions has rebounded, and a backlog for future deal opportunities remains “strong,” according to the firm’s report, published on Tuesday.

The forecast follows third-quarter (3Q) results from banks in which equity desks seized on an opening to outshine their debt counterparts. Geopolitical uncertainty stemming from President Donald Trump’s shifting policies, the war in the Middle East and changing interest-rate expectations have been a boon for stock traders amid the resulting market volatility.

See also: US stocks slide after hot inflation boosts December rate hike bets

Fixed-income trading desks, on the other hand, face fallout from rising interest rates, which can push down the value of existing debt and crimp demand from clients to transact or borrow. Incentive pay for debt traders is projected to be between 7.5% and 12.5%, less than half of their equity peers, according to the report. Those who help underwrite debt packages could see their pay rise an even smaller amount, between 5% and 10%.

The same dynamics affecting trading and underwriting results are also giving a boost to banks’ traditional roles as lenders, with some firms setting fresh records in 3Q for how much they earned from lending, with customers continuing to borrow even as interest rates increased.

Retail and commercial banking can be particularly vulnerable to changing rates. Bankers in those fields are poised to see their incentive pay rise up to 7.5%, Johnson Associates said, with lending activity edging higher and provisions for credit losses lower as questions around the Federal Reserve’s next rate move remain.

Advice can be top of mind in times of uncertainty in the market. Strong demand for wealth-management services is set to boost incentive pay for professionals in that business by as much as 12.5%. Similarly, those working in asset management could see a bump of as much as 14% on the back of market appreciation and inflows to active exchange-traded funds and alternative-investment vehicles.

Johnson’s expectations also echo what other industry reports have slated for payouts this year. A forecast last month by New York State Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli predicted that the Wall Street bonus pool will break records, with profit at broker-dealer firms that belong to the New York Stock Exchange on pace to exceed US$90 billion.

Recruitment firm Options Group said in a report that this year’s compensation would rise the most in equities, with a 15.6% gain from a year earlier. That compares to a 3% increase in investment banking and a 1.4% drop in fixed-income, credit and commodities trading.

“US banks are the outliers in the equities business. Even though European and Japanese banks did well, they didn’t capitalise like the US banks,” Michael Karp, Options Group’s chief executive officer, said in an interview. If similar market conditions persist into next year, “then 2027 could be a banner year as well.”

Full-year compensation may still change, especially with uncertainty around artificial intelligence (AI), interest rates and geopolitics. US banks will start compensation conversations in the coming weeks, with bonuses set to be paid out early in the new year.

When times are good and money is plentiful, individual windfalls can stretch into the millions of dollars, well above what bankers and traders reap from their salaries. Still, some banks may choose to exercise restraint, keeping a lid on their spending as analysts and investors raise questions around rising costs.

AI is also poised to change the way payouts are structured and companies reward their employees. The biggest Wall Street firms that have been more aggressive in managing head count and expenses may reward their employees with even more lucrative compensation, according to Chris Connors, managing director at Johnson Associates.

“The idea is it’s a bigger pie for fewer heads,” he said in a Bloomberg Television interview Tuesday. “It will probably be smaller analyst classes going forward, attrition without replacement and hopefully top-line growth.”

title: Fed’s Logan favours at least two hikes, says pace could quicken
article:
(Nov 11): Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas president Lorie Logan said she still sees the need for at least two quarter-point rate increases, but that the pace of those hikes may need to be quicker than the Fed is moving this fall.

“It remains clear to me, given the current outlook, that the FOMC needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases,” Logan said on Tuesday in prepared remarks for a conference in Houston, referring to the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on which she votes this year.

While the pace of hikes will depend on economic data and financial conditions, “It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the FOMC has moved so far this fall,” Logan added.

Fed officials left interest rates unchanged at their Oct 27-28 meeting after raising them by a quarter percentage point in September. That was the first rate hike since 2023 as policymakers seek to cool inflation that has been above their 2% target for more than five years.

A majority of officials in September signalled at least one more rate increase would be necessary this year, according to their median projection. While several Fed officials have reinforced this view in recent remarks and said hikes can come at a gradual pace, governor Christopher Waller earlier on Tuesday said the Fed should consider raising rates by a larger, half percentage point at its next meeting in December.

A report released on Tuesday morning showed the consumer price index rose by more than expected in October, with core inflation accelerating at a 0.3% pace from a month earlier. Logan said she’s concerned the Fed’s preferred gauge for inflation, due later this month, could show a similar pickup for October.

title: IBM to end immigration sponsorship for roles in biggest unit
article:
(Nov 11): International Business Machines Corp (IBM) is ending immigration sponsorship for some roles in its largest division following a crackdown by the Trump administration on a visa programme that’s been a talent pipeline for the tech industry.

“We have opted to discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of such roles in IBM Consulting,” an IBM spokesperson said.

Impacted workers can continue working with IBM outside the US, or leave the company at the end of the year, according to a document shared with managers this week in that division seen by Bloomberg. Consulting is by far IBM’s largest division, with over 150,000 workers, according to its website.

The technology industry’s reliance on foreign workers has long been a flashpoint in the debate over immigration. Since President Donald Trump’s return to office last year, the administration has seized on those concerns and pressed tech giants to do more to train and hire US workers.

As part of that effort, Trump has moved to make it harder for companies to use H-1B visas to attract foreign talent. The changes have included proposals for US$100,000 filing fees for most candidates and tightening the rules of how the H-1B visas are awarded in an annual lottery, giving priority to companies offering the highest salaries.

See also: US stocks slide after hot inflation boosts December rate hike bets

Last month the administration accused Microsoft Corp, Adobe Inc and a half-dozen other companies of abusing a US worker visa programme and suspended them indefinitely from using it.

The affected IBM division participated “US high-skilled visa programmes” to address skill shortages, the spokesperson said. But participation has been declining for a number of years and skill availability and client need have evolved, the spokesperson said.

Big Blue has refashioned itself as a high-growth software company through major acquisitions of Red Hat, HashiCorp and Confluent. At the same time, its consulting business has lagged — the division’s growth has been largely flat since 2024.
